teaching.causalExplanation: In Year 11 you localised the goals: start from a local need, and act across the Ottawa action areas. The syllabus names one body that did this: Healthy Cities Illawarra. Treat it as a model, not a list of projects. Since 1987, it has been a community-based organisation working on the conditions that produce health, not on treating illness. It works by convening, bringing councils, health services, schools, businesses and community groups together on local priorities. Its work maps onto the four goals. Food security, activity and social connection are SDG 3. School programs and helping people take part are SDG 4. Focusing on groups usually left out is SDG 10. And walking and cycling routes, community gardens and speaking up in planning decisions are SDG 11. One body, working on all four, because a community's problems don't arrive sorted by goal. So what transfers isn't any single project. It's having an independent, local, long-lasting body whose job is to hold the connections between sectors. Across successful community approaches, the same features keep appearing, and five are already on your strategy checklist. The community sets the priority, not just commenting on a plan already written. It works across sectors, because health alone can't change housing, transport or food. It changes conditions, not just behaviour. A footpath keeps working when the campaign stops. It lasts long enough, because conditions built over a decade won't shift in a two-year project. And it measures, by group. Two features are new lines. It works in settings people already use, like schools, workplaces and clubs. And it builds local capacity, so skills stay when funding ends. The usual barrier isn't willingness. It's funding. Short, competitive grants push groups toward small, visible projects and away from the slow work that changes outcomes. Four more patterns, each with its mechanism. Community-controlled health services are run by the communities they serve. Care designed by the people using it feels safe, so it's used, and chronic conditions get managed early. School programs reach every child without a family having to seek anything out. Whole-of-town food and activity changes alter what's on offer, so the easy option becomes the healthy one. And local advocacy gets health considered when transport routes, shops and open space are decided, when change is nearly free, not after. All four share one shape. Reach people where they are, change conditions instead of urging, and put the community inside the decision.

scenes.teachingReason: In Year 11 you localised the goals: start from a local need, and act across the Ottawa action areas. The syllabus names one body that did this: Healthy Cities Illawarra. Treat it as a model, not a list of projects. Since 1987, it has been a community-based organisation working on the conditions that produce health, not on treating illness. It works by convening, bringing councils, health services, schools, businesses and community groups together on local priorities. Its work maps onto the four goals. Food security, activity and social connection are SDG 3. School programs and helping people take part are SDG 4. Focusing on groups usually left out is SDG 10. And walking and cycling routes, community gardens and speaking up in planning decisions are SDG 11. One body, working on all four, because a community's problems don't arrive sorted by goal. So what transfers isn't any single project. It's having an independent, local, long-lasting body whose job is to hold the connections between sectors.

scenes.teachingReason: Across successful community approaches, the same features keep appearing, and five are already on your strategy checklist. The community sets the priority, not just commenting on a plan already written. It works across sectors, because health alone can't change housing, transport or food. It changes conditions, not just behaviour. A footpath keeps working when the campaign stops. It lasts long enough, because conditions built over a decade won't shift in a two-year project. And it measures, by group. Two features are new lines. It works in settings people already use, like schools, workplaces and clubs. And it builds local capacity, so skills stay when funding ends. The usual barrier isn't willingness. It's funding. Short, competitive grants push groups toward small, visible projects and away from the slow work that changes outcomes.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's why involving the community actually works. Community-led means the community sets the priorities and the design, not just comments on someone else's plan. Remember the ladder from Year 11: being consulted isn't leading. It finds the real problem: data shows a rate, but locals know the bus stops at six and the shop has closed. It's used, because people helped design it. It lasts, because the community owns it. And having control over decisions that affect your life is good for health in its own right. So the process is part of the intervention. But be honest about the catch. It's slower, it needs time and skills people may not have unpaid, and the loudest voices can take over. So it has to be community-led, properly resourced, and deliberate about including the people usually left out.
